title: 1965 USAF KC-135 Wichita crash
summary: KC-135A Stratotanker took off from McConnell AFB at 9:28 a.m. on 16 January 1965 loaded with 31000 gallons jet fuel. Aircraft gained very little altitude and experienced large yaw. Crew attempted return to airport and dumped fuel. Aircraft made hard left bank and began to enter roll. Unable to recover, crashed into residential neighborhood at Piatt and 20th Street three minutes after takeoff. Impact and resulting explosion destroyed dozens of homes killing all 7 crew and 23 civilians.
probable_cause: Rudder control system malfunction which was impossible for crew to overcome. Parachute ingested into Number 1 engine possibly contributed.

title: LAN Chile 107
summary: LAN-Chile Flight 107, a Douglas DC-6B-404 on a scheduled international flight from Santiago to Buenos Aires, crashed into La Corona Mountain in the Las Melosas area of the Andes at flight level 120 on 6 February 1965, about 1,200 feet below the summit. All 88 occupants were killed, including 22 players and staff of Santiago's Antonio Varas football team traveling to a match in Montevideo. The accident investigation board attributed the crash to the pilot in command choosing a route that followed neither the approved flight plan nor the airline's operations manual, and it ruled that weather was not a factor.

title: Eastern Provincial Airways 102
summary: A Handley Page Herald broke up in flight near Musquodoboit while climbing from 11,500 to 12,000 feet in favorable weather conditions. Witnesses heard an unusual loud noise and saw the tail section and then the cockpit section break off before the wreckage crashed. Investigation revealed progressive internal corrosion on the underside of the fuselage that ultimately caused the skin to fail and be struck by a propeller, severing the structure.

title: British United Airways 1030X
summary: British United Airways Flight 1030X departed Paris-Orly for Jersey Airport with 27 passengers and crew. Poor visibility and low cloud cover at Jersey made it difficult to see the runway. The crew aborted the first landing attempt. On the second approach, the aircraft's starboard wing struck the outermost pole of the approach lighting system at 58 feet altitude, 3000 feet short of the runway threshold. The impact severed the starboard wing, the aircraft rolled upside down and caught fire.

title: 1965 Little Baldon Hastings accident
summary: A Handley Page Hastings C1A transport aircraft crashed shortly after takeoff from RAF Abingdon with all 41 people aboard killed. The aircraft exhibited control difficulties including weaving side to side, wing waggling, and tail wobbling before climbing steeply out of control and diving into a field. Investigation found metal fatigue of two bolts in the elevator system. The failure of the upper bolts applied force on the starboard bracket, causing the lower bolts to also fail and a portion of the elevator to fail.

title: Canadian Pacific Air Lines 21
summary: Canadian Pacific Air Lines Flight 21, a Douglas DC-6B, crashed after an in-flight explosion on July 8, 1965. While en route from Vancouver to Prince George at approximately 15:40, three mayday calls were heard by air traffic control. An explosion had occurred in the left aft lavatory. The tail separated from the fuselage, the aircraft spiraled and crashed into a wooded area near 100 Mile House, British Columbia, killing all 52 people aboard.
probable_cause: A coroner's inquest concluded that an explosive substance foreign to the normal contents of the aircraft caused the crash. Traces of potassium nitrate and carbon consistent with a low-velocity explosion such as gunpowder or stumping powder were found. The perpetrator and motive remain undetermined.

The fuselage was consumed by fire where it fell, though the tail found 500 metres away was not burned.

title: British European Airways 706 (1965)
summary: British European Airways Flight 706 departed from Edinburgh Turnhouse Airport at 23:17 on 26 October 1965 on a scheduled flight to London Heathrow. During approach to runway 28R with fog reducing visibility to less than 50 metres, the aircraft overshot the runway twice and entered a hold. On the final approach, the crew decided to overshoot with the nose up and reducing flaps. The aircraft crashed 2,600 feet from the threshold and burst into flames. Investigation attributed the crash to pilot error with contributing factors including low visibility, pilot fatigue, anxiety, lack of experience in fog landing, and procedural errors.

title: American Airlines 383
summary: American Airlines Flight 383, a Boeing 727 carrying 57 passengers and 5 crew, was cleared for a visual approach to Cincinnati on November 8, 1965 in deteriorating weather with low visibility. The aircraft descended more rapidly than it should have without either pilot noticing, descending to just 3 feet above the airport while still 3 nautical miles away. The aircraft flew into wooded slopes in the Ohio River valley and crashed. Only three passengers and one flight attendant survived.

title: United Airlines 227
summary: United Airlines Flight 227 crashed short of runway 34L at Salt Lake City while conducting a high and fast unstable approach. The crew descended at approximately 2300 feet per minute, nearly triple the recommended rate, remaining 2000 feet above the normal glideslope at the outer marker. The captain rejected the first officer's attempt to add thrust with only seconds remaining before impact. The aircraft struck the runway with 4.7g vertical acceleration, rupturing fuel lines and causing post-impact fire that turned an initially survivable crash fatal, with 43 killed and 48 survivors.

title: Aeroflot 99
summary: Tupolev Tu-124 operating scheduled service from Leningrad-Pulkovo to Murmansk descended through poor weather with snow and 1.5 km visibility on 11 November 1965. title: Japan Airlines 813
summary: Japan Air Lines Flight 813, a Douglas DC-8 with 41 occupants, experienced an uncontained failure of its number one engine shortly after takeoff from San Francisco International Airport on 25 December 1965.
